director.chapterArc: Resolution and redefinition; Callie moves from physical exhaustion to a quiet realization of her unique power's mechanics (letting go) and establishes agency for her future at Meridian.
director.restraintNote: Maintain the narrator's grounded, observational distance. Do not dramatize Katori's diagnosis or Pell's arithmetic. The emotional weight lies in Callie's internal shift from 'holding on' to 'trusting', which must be delivered with quiet clarity rather than theatrical revelation.

cues.delivery: Katori's touch is the first real contact Callie has felt in days; convey relief and physical grounding without melodrama.
cues.from: Katori got to her first, and Katori's hand did not stop a finger's width off anything.
cues.through: It came down flat on Callie's shoulder, hard and thin and real, and stayed there. Callie lay in the road and felt it. There was ash on it. There was grey ash all the way up Katori's arm to the elbow and across the back of her hand, and it was the best thing Callie had felt since the dew outside the pump house.
cues.reason: Shift from action to intimate medical assessment.

cues.delivery: Katori's diagnosis is factual and dry; the horror of 'hate every breath' must be stated plainly.
cues.from: "There," said Katori. "And the next one, probably. Cracked. Not broken through, or you'd not be breathing even halfway, and you'd know it." She sat back on her heels. "You'll live. You'll hate every breath for three weeks, and you'll live."
cues.through: "Is at the top of the pitch, chocked, and Pell's sitting on the tailboard with his head in his hands. The horse is two hundred paces up the road with Otto hanging off her neck. Three husks are ash on the high plain." Katori looked at her. "You could have called me."

cues.delivery: Callie's laughter is a release of tension; it should sound fragile and physical ('stabbing pieces'), not joyful.
cues.from: "You'd have come fifty paces," said Callie, "and it'd have been on me before you got ten." She shut her eyes. "And you were lit. You lit yourself. On purpose. I saw your Ember come out."
cues.through: Callie laughed. It was a very bad idea. She lay in the road and held her left side and tried not to laugh, and laughed anyway, in small stabbing pieces. Katori sat beside her and did not help at all.
cues.reason: Emotional pivot from pain to shared relief.

cues.delivery: Mother's voice is steady and practical; the warmth comes from her competence in a crisis.
cues.from: "I know. I saw it. I was the one who told you." Her mother's thumb moved once across her forehead. "I'm not complaining. I'm just saying, for the record, that for about a minute and a half there you did exactly as you were told. It's the first time since you were four, and I want it written down somewhere."
cues.through: "I haven't looked yet," said her mother. "I'm asking about the needle so that you'll lie still while I look, because you'll be too busy being frightened of it to move." She bent over Callie's head. "Hold still, love. It's only a scalp. Scalps bleed. It's what they're for."
cues.reason: Shift to maternal authority during medical procedure.

cues.delivery: Pell's ledger reading must be precise and rhythmic; the addition of 'T' is a quiet but significant act of validation.
cues.from:
Pitch. Two pulls, tackle, C.'s hook in the seam. Ninety-one seconds.
C.'s call. Concur — K., P., I., O.
cues.through: "It's in the book," Pell agreed, and shut it.
cues.reason: Logistical closure to the physical struggle.

cues.delivery: The horse's approach is a moment of suspended tension; read the physical description with slow, deliberate pacing.
cues.from: She was dark. She had nothing in her at all. The well was dry to the stone, with not even a finger mark of damp at the bottom. There was nothing on her anywhere that a horse or a husk or anything else in the world could feel. She was a girl with her ribs bound in a blanket, sitting against a rock.
cues.through: "She hauled," said Otto. His voice was wrecked from shouting. "She hauled it all. She went, and I pointed her, and she hauled it, and she — " He stopped, and wiped his face on his shoulder, and left a long streak of dirt across it. "I thought she was going to go over the side. I thought I'd lost her. She didn't. She went where I pointed."

cues.delivery: Pell's naming of the horse is a dry, matter-of-fact decision; avoid sentimentality.
cues.from: "Nobody ever knows," said Pell. "That's the whole trade." He looked at the mare for a long moment in the last of the light. Then he said, in the voice he used for distances, "Duchess."
cues.through: "Her name," said Pell, "is Duchess. I've decided. Don't look at me like that, Otto, I'm sixty-one and I'm allowed to change my mind once a decade, and this is the once." He turned back to the wagon. "Now get her rubbed down before she stiffens, and see to that leg, and somebody find me my hat."

cues.delivery: Ines's observation is a factual report; the realization that the hook was brighter than Callie must be delivered with quiet weight.
cues.from: "When it hit the hook," said Ines. "The husk. It went a hand's width left at the last. Away from you. Toward the hook."

cues.delivery: The atmosphere is quiet and reflective; Katori's request for information should feel like a necessary inventory.
cues.from: Everyone else was asleep, or pretending to be, round the fire in the lee of the wagon at the top of the pitch. Callie's mother was under two blankets on the wagon bed. She had been asleep since an hour after sunset and she had gone to sleep all at once, in the middle of a sentence, the way the lamp goes out when the oil is gone. Her borrowed day was spent. Callie had watched it go out of her face as the sun went down, the colour first, then the straightness, then the words. She had been wanting all evening to ask Katori if that was what it looked like when you paid a borrowed day back. She did not ask, because she did not want to know yet.
cues.through: "Tell me what you know," said Katori. "Now. While it's fresh. I want to hear you say it, all of it, and I'll tell you if it sounds like anything."

cues.delivery: Callie's explanation of the power mechanics is analytical; 'drier than the pump house' should sound like a physical fact.
cues.from: "It holds as long as I don't hold it. I don't understand that one. But it's true. If I grip it, it drains out of me like two buckets. If I let it stand, and don't look at it, and don't argue with it, it stands." She breathed halfway in. "Ninety-one seconds today, and that was all of me. There's nothing left. I'm drier than the pump house."

cues.delivery: Katori's realization about 'holding' is a quiet epiphany; the tone should be one of shared discovery.
cues.from: "Then it's still you," she said. "Whatever you put in that hook, it's you. You didn't make a tool. You put yourself in the steel." She looked into the fire. "I don't know if that's what my grandmother meant by light. I don't know if it's what anybody means by anything. But I know I've had this" — she touched her coat, where the slab was — "for eleven years. And in eleven years nobody has ever taught me one single thing about my own door that I didn't already know. And today you did. Twice."
cues.through: Callie did not say anything. She had a strong sense that she was not meant to, and that she had been told something she would not understand for years. So she said nothing, and let it be.

cues.delivery: The description of the light is vast and distant; read with a sense of scale and cold clarity.
cues.from: It was Pell who saw the light. He saw it because he was the one who could not sleep. He was sitting up on the tailboard with the atlas on his knee, looking north, the way Katori always looked north.
cues.through: "That's it," said Pell. "That's the only thing between here and the sea that's lit like that."

cues.delivery: Callie's thought of her mother is internal and somber; the distance calculation should feel heavy.
cues.from: Callie thought of her mother asleep on the boards behind her, who had gone out like a lamp at sunset. She thought of the plucking hand at two in the morning, and a minute and a bit more. Longer than the last one.
cues.through: Katori came and stood at the other side of her. For a while all three of them looked north at the light without speaking.

cues.delivery: Katori's explanation of Meridian is serious and explanatory; the concept of 'columns' must be delivered with gravity.
cues.from: "But I have to tell you what that means now. It meant one thing on the first morning, and it means something else tonight." Katori kept her eyes on the light. "When I stand for somebody at Meridian, I stand for what they are. I say, this is a girl I hired, a hunter, she reads ground better than anyone I've met, and she's good for it. And they write it down. They write everything down at that gate. Pell's not the only one with a book."
cues.through: "Meridian has columns," Katori agreed. "It's got a column for Ember people and a column for hand-tradition. It's got a column for people with no door at all, like Ines. It's got a column for hunters and one for lifters, and one for sick women who need a doctor." She was quiet for a moment. "It hasn't got a column for you. Nobody has. And the kind of people who make columns don't like a thing that doesn't fit in one. They make a new column for it. And then they decide what the column's for."

cues.delivery: Callie's decision to speak for herself is a quiet act of defiance; the voice should be steady and resolved.
cues.from: She thought about the jar at the bottom of the barrow. There had been five handfuls in it, and now there were four, because her mother had spent one on a hill. She thought about her tenth, in Pell's book, which had been more than the jar many times over. She had drunk most of it in three days, two fingers at a time, at the bottom of a scarp and on the top of one. She had drunk it to buy seventeen seconds, then forty-four, then ninety-one. It had been her gate money. It had been the thing she meant to put down on the table in front of the columns so that they would see she could pay.
cues.through: "When we get there," said Callie. "At the gate. When you stand for me. I'll tell them myself what goes in the column. Not you. Not Pell. Me." She was surprised by how steady her voice was. "I'll tell them what I want them to know, and not one thing more. I'll decide it before we get there, all of it. I've got nine days."

cues.delivery: The final realization of the well filling is subtle and internal; read with a sense of quiet hope.
cues.from: The well was dry. It was dry right down to the stone.
cues.through: It was filling. Slowly, on its own, the way Katori had said it would, it had begun to fill.

pauses.after: It came down flat on Callie's shoulder, hard and thin and real, and stayed there. Callie lay in the road and felt it. There was ash on it. There was grey ash all the way up Katori's arm to the elbow and across the back of her hand, and it was the best thing Callie had felt since the dew outside the pump house.
pauses.reason: Physical grounding after the first touch; reset for dialogue.
Emphasis on the physical sensation of ash after pain.

pauses.after: "There," said Katori. "And the next one, probably. Cracked. Not broken through, or you'd not be breathing even halfway, and you'd know it." She sat back on her heels. "You'll live. You'll hate every breath for three weeks, and you'll live."
pauses.reason: Completed thought on prognosis before shifting to wagon status.
Weighted statement of survival against odds.

pauses.reason: Pause for the emotional release of laughter and shared tension.
Highlighting the deliberate nature of Katori's action.

pauses.reason: Emphasizing the rarity and significance of compliance.

pauses.after: "I haven't looked yet," said her mother. "I'm asking about the needle so that you'll lie still while I look, because you'll be too busy being frightened of it to move." She bent over Callie's head. "Hold still, love. It's only a scalp. Scalps bleed. It's what they're for."
pauses.reason: End of medical instruction; transition to action (stitches).

pauses.after: Callie's mother leaned over and read it upside down and said nothing. After a moment she reached out with her left hand and took the pencil from behind Pell's ear. Slowly, left-handed, in letters that went a little crooked at the end, she wrote a single T. at the end of the line, as if signing for a parcel. Then she gave him the pencil back.
pauses.reason: Significant narrative beat: the mother's signature in the ledger.
Focus on the specific signature marking inclusion.

pauses.after: She was dark. She had nothing in her at all. The well was dry to the stone, with not even a finger mark of damp at the bottom. There was nothing on her anywhere that a horse or a husk or anything else in the world could feel. She was a girl with her ribs bound in a blanket, sitting against a rock.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on Callie's state of being 'dark' and vulnerable.
Highlighting the breakthrough in horse behavior.

pauses.after: "Six," she said, and put them in the quiver one at a time. She did not look at Callie. Then she stopped with the last one in her fingers, halfway to the quiver, and did look at her.
pauses.reason: Pause before Ines delivers the critical observation about the hook.

pauses.after: "That's how it goes," said Katori. "That's how it always goes, in the first year. You'll hate it for a long time." She was quiet for a while. "Is there anything else?"
pauses.reason: End of Callie's technical explanation; transition to Katori's response.

pauses.before: Whatever you put in that hook
pauses.reason: Defining the nature of Callie's connection to her power.

pauses.after: Callie did not say anything. She had a strong sense that she was not meant to, and that she had been told something she would not understand for years. So she said nothing, and let it be.
pauses.reason: Silence after the thematic realization about 'holding' before moving on.

pauses.after: It was not a fire. A fire moves. It was not a star either. It was too low, and too wide, and the wrong colour, a pale steady white like nothing she had ever seen. It sat on the edge of the world and lit the bottom of the clouds above it from underneath, very faintly. It did not flicker at all. It had not flickered, she understood, for seventy years.
pauses.reason: End of description; pause for Pell's identification of the light.
Emphasizing the age and stability of the light source.

pauses.after: "Seven days, on a good road with two good animals. We've got one, and she's lame." He licked the pencil. "Nine. Call it nine, and three ifs on top. Ten or eleven, and I'll be glad to be wrong."
pauses.reason: Calculation complete; transition to Callie's internal thought.
Pause before Katori reveals the deeper meaning of her promise.

pauses.before: It hasn't got a column for you.
pauses.reason: Highlighting Callie's unique and unclassified status.

pauses.after: What she had left to put on the table was what she was.
pauses.reason: End of Callie's internal accounting; setup for her declaration.
